prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

The usual procedure of including a finite number of vertices in Non Perturbative Renormalization Group equations in order to obtain $n$-point correlation functions at finite momenta is analyzed. This is done by exploiting a general method recently introduced which includes simultaneously all vertices although approximating their momentum dependence. The study is performed using the self-energy of the tridimensional scalar model at criticality. At least in this example, low order truncations miss quantities as the critical exponent $\eta$ by as much as 60%. However, if one goes to high order truncations the procedure seems to converge rapidly.

outputs.L1: The standard procedure of retaining a finite number of vertices in Non-Perturbative Renormalization Group equations to obtain \(n\)-point correlation functions at finite momenta is analyzed. This analysis is carried out using a recently introduced general method that simultaneously incorporates all vertices, while approximating their momentum dependence. The study focuses on the self-energy of the three-dimensional scalar model at criticality. In this example, at least, low-order truncations can miss quantities such as the critical exponent \(\eta\) by as much as 60%. However, when higher-order truncations are employed, the procedure appears to converge rapidly.
outputs.L2: A common strategy for deriving finite-momentum \(n\)-point correlation functions from Non-Perturbative Renormalization Group equations is to retain only a limited set of vertices. This approach is examined here by using a recently proposed general framework that treats all vertices at the same time, while making approximations to their momentum dependence. The analysis focuses on the self-energy of the three-dimensional scalar model at criticality. In this case, low-order truncations can give poor results, missing values such as the critical exponent \(\eta\) by up to 60%. By contrast, when higher-order truncations are used, the method appears to converge quickly.
outputs.L3:
The text examines a common approximation used in the Non-Perturbative Renormalization Group (NPRG) approach, namely the truncation of the exact flow equations to a finite number of vertices in order to compute finite-momentum \(n\)-point correlation functions. Since the full NPRG hierarchy contains infinitely many coupled equations, practical calculations often require closing the system by retaining only a limited subset of vertex functions. The reliability of this procedure, however, is not always clear, especially when one is interested in momentum-dependent quantities.

To assess this issue, the analysis relies on a recently introduced method that treats all vertex functions simultaneously, while using an approximation for their momentum dependence. This framework makes it possible to compare finite-order vertex truncations with a more complete treatment of the hierarchy, and therefore to evaluate how much accuracy is lost when only a small number of vertices is retained.

The study is carried out for the three-dimensional scalar field model at criticality, with particular attention paid to the self-energy. This quantity provides a useful testing ground because it depends nontrivially on momentum and is directly related to important critical properties of the theory.

The results show that low-order truncations can lead to significant inaccuracies. In particular, they may fail to reproduce key universal quantities correctly: the critical exponent \(\eta\), which characterizes the anomalous scaling of the two-point function, can be missed by as much as 60% in such approximations. This indicates that low-order vertex truncations may be insufficient for quantitatively reliable predictions of finite-momentum correlation functions.

On the other hand, the analysis also suggests that the situation improves substantially when higher-order truncations are included. In the example studied, the sequence of higher-order approximations appears to converge rapidly toward the result obtained from the more complete treatment. Thus, while low-order truncations can be misleading, sufficiently high-order vertex expansions may provide an efficient and accurate way to compute momentum-dependent correlation functions within the NPRG framework.
outputs.L4:
The text discusses the use of finite-vertex truncations within the framework of the Non Perturbative Renormalization Group (NPRG) to compute finite-momentum \(n\)-point correlation functions. In NPRG calculations, one often has to deal with an infinite hierarchy of coupled flow equations for correlation functions of all orders. In practice, this hierarchy must be truncated in order to make calculations feasible. The central question addressed by the text is how reliable such finite-vertex truncations are, especially when the goal is to determine correlation functions with nontrivial momentum dependence.

The work focuses on a relatively recent approximation scheme that improves on more traditional low-order truncations. Instead of keeping only a small number of vertices exactly and discarding the rest, this method includes contributions from all vertices, while approximating their momentum dependence in a controlled way. This makes it possible to go beyond the simplest truncation schemes and to examine how physical quantities change as increasingly high-order vertices are taken into account. The approach is applied to the self-energy of the three-dimensional scalar model at criticality, a standard test case for renormalization-group methods because of its connection to universal critical behavior.

A major goal of the analysis is to assess the convergence of the vertex expansion. The authors compare results obtained at different truncation orders and study how sensitive observables are to the inclusion of higher-order correlation functions. In particular, they examine the critical exponent \(\eta\), which characterizes the anomalous scaling of the two-point correlation function at criticality. This exponent is a demanding quantity to compute accurately because it is directly tied to the momentum dependence of the self-energy.

The results show that low-order truncations can be quantitatively unreliable. In some cases, truncations that keep only the first few vertices produce values of \(\eta\) that differ from the converged result by as much as 60%. This demonstrates that apparently reasonable low-order approximations may miss important contributions from higher-order vertices and can therefore lead to misleading conclusions about critical behavior.

At the same time, the study finds that the sequence of higher-order truncations appears to converge rapidly once sufficiently many vertices are included. This suggests that the newer NPRG approximation scheme provides a practical and systematically improvable route for computing finite-momentum correlation functions. The main conclusion is that finite-vertex truncations can be powerful, but only if they are pushed to high enough order. Reliance on very low-order truncations may severely underestimate or misrepresent key physical quantities, whereas sufficiently high-order treatments offer accurate and stable results for the critical properties of the model.
outputs.L5:
**The Non-Perturbative**

In physics and mathematics, the word **non-perturbative** refers to phenomena or methods that cannot be fully described by small corrections to a simple, known solution. In many scientific theories, especially in quantum field theory, researchers often use **perturbation theory**: they begin with an idealized system that can be solved exactly, then add small “perturbations” to approximate more complex behavior. This approach works well when interactions are weak.

However, not all systems are weakly interacting. Some effects are so strong, complex, or deeply collective that they cannot be captured by adding small corrections. These are called **non-perturbative** effects. They often reveal the most interesting and fundamental aspects of a theory.

A major example appears in **quantum chromodynamics** (QCD), the theory of quarks and gluons. At high energies, quarks interact weakly and perturbative methods are useful. But at low energies, the force becomes strong, and quarks are confined inside particles such as protons and neutrons. This confinement is a non-perturbative phenomenon. It cannot be understood simply by expanding around a weakly interacting system.

Non-perturbative methods are also important in string theory, condensed matter physics, statistical mechanics, and the study of phase transitions. Tools such as lattice simulations, instantons, solitons, dualities, and numerical techniques help scientists explore regimes where ordinary perturbative calculations fail.

The non-perturbative is therefore not just a technical category. It represents the boundary between what can be approximated easily and what requires deeper insight. It is often where hidden structures, new phases of matter, and profound physical principles emerge. In this sense, non-perturbative physics reminds us that some truths cannot be reached by small steps alone; they require a different way of seeing the whole system.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a concise abstract for a physics paper about finite-vertex truncations in Non Perturbative Renormalization Group equations and their accuracy for computing momentum-dependent n-point functions.
counterfactuals.output: We investigate the accuracy of finite-vertex truncations in Non-Perturbative Renormalization Group (NPRG) equations for computing momentum-dependent \(n\)-point correlation functions. By closing the exact hierarchy of flow equations at finite order, such truncations provide a practical route to nonperturbative momentum-resolved observables, but their reliability depends sensitively on the retained vertex content and momentum structure. We analyze the convergence of successive truncation levels and quantify their impact on propagators and higher \(n\)-point functions across representative regimes. Our results show that finite-vertex schemes can reproduce the dominant momentum dependence with controlled accuracy when supplemented by consistent feedback between lower- and higher-order vertices, while overly local or low-order closures may miss important nontrivial structures. These findings clarify the domain of validity of vertex expansion strategies in NPRG and provide practical criteria for systematic improvement.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Summarize a study evaluating low- and high-order vertex truncations in NPRG using the self-energy of the three-dimensional scalar model at criticality, including the effect on the critical exponent eta.
counterfactuals.output:
The study uses the **three-dimensional one-component scalar (Ising) model at criticality** as a benchmark for testing **vertex truncations** in the nonperturbative renormalization group (NPRG). The main observable is the full momentum-dependent **self-energy** \(\Sigma(p)\), or equivalently the inverse two-point function, which at criticality should scale as

\[
\Gamma^{(2)}(p) \sim p^{2-\eta},
\]

where \(\eta\) is the anomalous dimension.

### Main idea

The authors compare NPRG approximations in which the infinite hierarchy of flow equations for \(n\)-point vertices is truncated at different orders:

- **Low-order vertex truncations**, retaining only a small number of vertices, e.g. up to the four-point function.
- **Higher-order truncations**, including more vertices and field dependences, intended to better approximate the full hierarchy.

The self-energy at criticality is a sensitive test because its momentum dependence encodes the anomalous scaling exponent \(\eta\).

### Findings on the self-energy

Low-order truncations reproduce the qualitative behavior of the critical self-energy, especially the crossover between small- and large-momentum regimes, but they are not quantitatively reliable over the full scaling range. In particular, the momentum dependence of \(\Sigma(p)\) can be distorted because the neglected higher vertices feed back into the flow of the two-point function.

Higher-order truncations improve the scaling form of the self-energy and give a more stable momentum dependence. As more vertices or higher field orders are included, the calculated self-energy converges toward the expected critical behavior.

### Effect on the anomalous dimension \(\eta\)

The critical exponent \(\eta\) is especially sensitive to the truncation. Low-order vertex truncations tend to give less stable estimates and can overestimate or otherwise shift \(\eta\) relative to accurate benchmark values.

Including higher-order vertices reduces this truncation dependence. The resulting values of \(\eta\) move closer to the accepted three-dimensional Ising value,

\[
\eta \simeq 0.036,
\]

and become more stable under further improvements of the truncation.

### Overall conclusion

The study shows that the NPRG vertex expansion can describe the critical self-energy of the three-dimensional scalar model, but **low-order truncations are not sufficient for high quantitative accuracy**, particularly for the anomalous dimension. **Higher-order vertex truncations significantly improve the self-energy scaling and stabilize the estimate of \(\eta\)**, demonstrating the importance of vertex feedback in NPRG calculations at criticality.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Draft an academic-style paragraph explaining how a recently introduced NPRG method that includes all vertices with approximate momentum dependence can be used to analyze convergence of n-point correlation function calculations.
counterfactuals.output: A recently introduced nonperturbative renormalization group (NPRG) scheme that retains the full hierarchy of vertices while approximating their momentum dependence provides a useful framework for assessing the convergence of calculations of \(n\)-point correlation functions. In standard NPRG formulations, the exact flow equation for a given vertex function \(\Gamma_k^{(n)}\) is coupled to higher-order vertices, generating an infinite hierarchy that must be truncated in practical applications. The new method improves on conventional truncations by keeping all vertices in the flow equations and introducing a controlled approximation for their momentum dependence, thereby reducing the bias associated with omitting higher-order functions altogether. This makes it possible to compare successive levels of approximation in a systematic way: one can monitor how the computed two-, four-, and higher-point functions change as increasingly detailed momentum structures are included. Convergence can then be analyzed by examining the stability of physical observables, scaling dimensions, anomalous dimensions, and vertex functions under refinement of the approximation. Because the approach preserves the coupled structure of the NPRG hierarchy more faithfully than low-order truncations, it offers a direct means of identifying which momentum-dependent contributions are essential and which are subleading. Consequently, this method provides both a practical computational tool for evaluating \(n\)-point correlation functions and a diagnostic framework for quantifying the reliability and convergence of NPRG-based approximations.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a brief research abstract stating that common finite-vertex truncation schemes in non-perturbative RG equations can significantly underestimate the anomalous dimension in the 3D critical scalar model but improve at higher orders.
counterfactuals.output: Common finite-vertex truncation schemes in non-perturbative renormalization group equations are assessed for the three-dimensional critical scalar model. By comparing successive truncation orders, we find that low-order vertex expansions can significantly underestimate the anomalous dimension, indicating that important momentum- and field-dependent contributions are not fully captured. Nevertheless, the estimates systematically improve as higher-order vertices are included, showing convergence toward more accurate critical behavior. These results highlight both the limitations of low-order truncations and the practical value of systematically extended non-perturbative RG schemes for precision studies of critical phenomena.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: In formal scientific language, describe an analysis of the standard practice of retaining only finitely many vertices in NPRG equations for finite-momentum correlation functions, mentioning results for the self-energy and critical exponent $\eta$.
counterfactuals.output:
An analysis was performed of the commonly employed truncation strategy in nonperturbative renormalization-group equations for finite-momentum correlation functions, in which only a finite number of vertex functions is retained. Within this framework, the infinite hierarchy of exact flow equations for the one-particle irreducible vertices is closed by discarding, or approximating, higher-order vertices beyond a prescribed order.

The study shows that such finite-vertex truncations can provide a controlled and quantitatively reliable description of the momentum dependence of low-order correlation functions, provided that the retained vertices are treated with sufficient consistency. In particular, the momentum-dependent self-energy obtained from the truncated flow reproduces the expected scaling behavior in the critical regime. At criticality, the self-energy behaves as

\[
\Sigma(p) \sim p^{2-\eta},
\]

where \(\eta\) is the anomalous dimension. The analysis demonstrates that the finite-truncation procedure yields a nonzero anomalous exponent and captures the crossover between the small-momentum critical regime and the large-momentum perturbative regime.

The resulting estimates of the critical exponent \(\eta\) are found to be in good agreement with values obtained from more refined NPRG schemes and from other nonperturbative methods. This supports the conclusion that, although the exact NPRG hierarchy involves infinitely many coupled vertex functions, retaining only finitely many vertices can still constitute an accurate approximation for finite-momentum observables, including the self-energy and the associated anomalous scaling exponent.
